title: How would you estimate the size of the UK gym membership market?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How big is the UK gym membership market each year?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: A clean estimate puts the UK gym membership market at about $6.7B a year: roughly 10 million members paying an average of $55 a month. Industry data puts the real figure higher, at about $8.5B, and working out why is the most useful part of this question. Try your own estimate before you read on.
body:
The question

How big is the UK gym membership market each year?

Gyms are a good one for practising sanity checks. The chain is short (people, share with a membership, monthly fee), but the average fee hides a market split between budget chains, council leisure centres and premium clubs. Get the mix wrong and the answer drifts.

Clarify before you calculate

  • Value or members? Value: membership fees per year, in dollars.
  • Which gyms? Private clubs (budget to premium) and public-sector leisure centres. Exclude boutique studios sold per class unless the interviewer wants them.
  • Which price? What members actually pay after discounts, not the list price on the website.

Rough guess: "Several billion dollars. Gyms are on every high street and many people pay monthly."

Step by step

  1. People in the UK: 68M.
  2. Share with a gym membership: 15% → 68M × 15% = 10.2M members.
  3. Average monthly fee: build it from the mix rather than guessing one number.
SegmentShare of membersMonthly feeContribution
Budget chains45%$30$13.50
Mid-market and council gyms40%$55$22.00
Premium clubs15%$130$19.50

Weighted average: $55 a month. Notice that premium clubs are only 15% of members but over a third of the average fee.

Market: 10.2M × $55 × 12 = about $6.7B a year.

Sanity check from a second angle

Supply side

Count gyms instead of people. Assume about 7,000 gyms in the UK with an average of 1,500 members each: 7,000 × 1,500 = 10.5M members. That is within 3% of the demand-side figure, so the member count looks sound.

Real-world check

The Leisure Database Company's 2025 State of the UK Fitness Industry report counts 7,202 gyms, a penetration rate of 16.6% and about 11.3M members (7.8M in private clubs, 3.5M in public-sector gyms). It values the market at 6.5 billion in pounds, about $8.5B at an exchange rate of $1.30. It puts the average private-club fee at the equivalent of about $63 a month and public-sector fees at about $43.

Our $6.7B is about 20% below that. Two assumptions explain the gap: penetration is 16.6% rather than 15%, and the real average fee is higher than $55. That is exactly what a sanity check is for: it tells you which assumption to revisit. Source: Leisure Opportunities: LeisureDB 2025 report summary.

Which assumption matters most

The average fee. A 10% rise, from $55 to $60.50, lifts the market to 10.2M × $60.50 × 12 = about $7.4B with no change in members. Because premium clubs carry so much of the average, a small shift in the mix between budget and premium moves the total more than a small shift in penetration.

For a client, the market number is only the start. A gym chain cares about its reachable market: local population × share who join gyms × achievable market share × revenue per member, then capacity at peak hours and how long members stay.

What a strong answer sounds like

"68 million people, about 15% with a membership, is roughly 10 million members. Fees vary a lot, so I'll blend budget at $30, mid-market at $55 and premium at $130, which averages about $55 a month. That's around $6.7 billion a year. Seven thousand gyms with 1,500 members each gives a similar member count. The fee mix is the assumption I'd test first, because premium clubs drive a third of the average."

A weak answer uses one fee for everyone, often a budget price, and never asks who the members are. It will understate the market and cannot explain why.

Common mistakes

  • One price for a split market. Budget and premium gyms are different businesses. Blend them.
  • List price instead of realised price. Joining offers, corporate discounts and frozen memberships pull real revenue below the advertised fee.
  • Members versus visitors. Pay-as-you-go users and class passes are not monthly members. Agree what is in scope.

Practice

1. How big is the budget gym segment?

Show the answer

45% of 10.2M = about 4.6M members × $30 × 12 = about $1.65B a year, roughly a quarter of the market from nearly half the members.

2. A budget chain opens in a town of 100,000 adults with three rival gyms. What revenue could it expect?

Show the answer

100,000 × 16% gym-goers = 16,000. With four gyms, assume a quarter share: 4,000 members × $30 × 12 = about $1.4M a year, before checking peak-hour capacity.
